title: Perturb and Correct: Post-Hoc Ensembles using Affine Redundancy
claim: Perturbing a hidden layer and refitting the next layer keeps predictions matched in-distribution while letting them diverge out-of-distribution.
layout: 2 rows, left-to-right flow, colored operator badges between rows, ID/OOD bars at right
description: A two-row block diagram flowing left to right. An input box on the far left splits into two paths. The top row is the original network: an original layer, a following affine layer, and a prediction ŷ, in green and pink boxes. The bottom row is the modified network: an orange perturbed layer, a purple corrected affine layer, and a prediction ŷ_new. An orange '+' badge labeled 'parameter perturbation' joins the original and perturbed layers vertically. A purple 'LS' badge labeled 'least-squares correction' joins the two affine layers. At the far right, each row has a small bar chart of ‖Δy‖/‖Δh‖ for ID (green) and OOD (red). The top row shows both bars tall. The bottom row shows a short ID bar and a tall OOD bar. The eye goes to the colored badges and then to the bar contrast.
caption: Perturb-and-Correct. A hidden-layer perturbation changes the representation $h$ to $h_v$. The following affine layer is refitted on ID calibration examples so that the corrected predictor remains close to the base model there. At a shifted input, the representation change may not be reconstructed from the changes observed on calibration data, leaving a post-correction residual that can produce ensemble disagreement.
abstract: Models that are nearly indistinguishable on in-distribution data can behave very differently under distribution shift. We introduce Perturb-and-Correct (P&C), a post-hoc method for constructing epistemically diverse predictors from a single pretrained network. P&C applies random hidden-layer perturbations with a least-squares correction in the following affine layer, producing predictors that agree on calibration data while remaining free to disagree away from it. We analyze this mechanism through the post-correction residual that remains in the activation of the layer corrected using calibration data, yielding a leverage-based preservation bound and a covariance interpretation of ensemble disagreement. Empirically, P&C achieves a strong ID/OOD tradeoff across MuJoCo dynamics prediction and CIFAR-10 OOD detection, and scales to a pretrained ViT-B/16 on ImageNet-1K. In matched comparisons with Deep Ensembles, P&C substantially reduces construction and storage cost. Our findings highlight the potential in further exploiting overparameterization as a strength of deep learning models.
